script.text: Three American aircraft carriers off Iran. Russian missiles on the ground in Poland, a NATO country. And on Saturday night, Iran's Revolutionary Guards say they fired at U.S. bases in Bahrain. All in one week.

Five stories, ranked by impact. Tanks across a ceasefire line in Gaza. A rebel army closing in on the city that hosts Yemen's government. Three nuclear powers signing one short text in China. A war that crossed into NATO territory. And at number one, an island where more than fourteen tankers are reportedly lined up, waiting.

Number five: Gaza's Yellow Line. On Wednesday, Israeli tanks pushed west of that line in central Gaza. Reuters and AFP reported it was the first ground push past the ceasefire boundary since the truce began in October twenty twenty-five. The Israeli military and the Shin Bet said the target was a Hamas tunnel near the Nuseirat and Bureij camps. Residents were ordered out. Witnesses told Reuters some tanks reached Salah al-Din Road, the main north to south highway. Hamas called it a flagrant violation of the ceasefire and asked the mediators to step in. On Thursday, the tanks pulled back. The army told AFP the operation was completed and the road had reopened. By then, AFP reports, about six thousand Palestinians had fled their shelters. Al Jazeera reports that the Yellow Line has been moved step by step, and now takes in around two thirds of the enclave. Gaza's health authorities say more than one thousand six hundred Palestinians have been killed since it began. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have died. A Board of Peace report to the U.N. Security Council, seen by Reuters, faults both sides: Israel for restricting aid, Hamas for armed activity. For you, the line decides where Gaza's people can live, and where aid trucks can drive. Next: a rebel army closing in on Yemen's interim capital.

Number four: Yemen. On the fifteenth, Yemen's Saudi-backed government said its forces had pulled back from Dhubab and other areas near the Bab al-Mandab strait, to defend Aden, the government's interim capital. Five Yemeni military officials told Reuters the Houthis had reached Khor Omairah, about one hundred kilometres west of the city. AFP military sources put them closer, within about sixty kilometres. The front line itself could not be independently verified. A day later, a Saudi royal decree replaced the commander of the coalition's joint forces. Reuters reports the Houthis have gained ground since the Iran war revived Yemen's civil war this summer. Then the fighting reached Saudi Arabia again. On Friday, Saudi-led strikes hit Houthi positions in Sanaa and Hodeidah, Gulf News reports. Early on Saturday, the coalition said it intercepted three ballistic missiles fired toward Riyadh. Not everyone expects an assault on Aden. A Yemeni security official told The National an attack was unlikely, and the Houthis say they do not intend to attack the city. Why it matters to you: the Bab al-Mandab is the southern gate of the Red Sea. Ships between Asia and Europe pass it on the way to the Suez Canal. Next: three leaders, one text, and two wars left out.

Number three: Shenzhen. On Thursday, Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin met together for the first time, on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China. They signed a short text called the Declaration toward Peace. Its key line: a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. The three promise dialogue on nuclear risk reduction and non-proliferation. Reuters notes there is no date and no format for those talks. The text also backs more refined petroleum products and stable energy flows, an unspecified reform of the United Nations, and warns international courts not to abuse their jurisdiction. The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Putin in March twenty twenty-three. Quick question. When did New START, the last treaty capping American and Russian nuclear warheads, expire? Take a guess. The answer: February twenty twenty-six. Since then, no treaty limits the two biggest arsenals. Russia holds nearly five thousand five hundred warheads, the United States about five thousand two hundred, and China about six hundred, according to the Federation of American Scientists. What the text leaves out matters too. Ukraine and Iran are not mentioned. Trump called the meeting bigger than Yalta. Xi called the talks positive, constructive and fruitful. And in Shenzhen, Putin said that after the strikes on the Crimean Bridge, Russia would not negotiate a ceasefire. For you, it means that for now, nothing on paper limits the world's largest nuclear arsenals. Next: the bridge he meant.

Number two: the war that crossed into NATO territory. It started with a bridge. On the sixteenth and seventeenth, Ukraine struck the Kerch Bridge, Russia's road and rail link to occupied Crimea. Footage geolocated by CNN and NBC News showed a road span collapsed into the water. Ukraine's security service said a steel arch and the road span were destroyed. Russia halted all traffic, and the business daily Vedomosti later reported one rail track had reopened. Then Russia struck back. Overnight into Friday, it launched one of the war's biggest attacks. Zelensky counted more than four hundred drones and over one hundred and ten missiles. In Kyiv, three bridges over the Dnipro were hit. At least eight people were killed across Ukraine, AP reports. Russia's defence ministry said the bridges were used to move weapons. And then, Poland. Two Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone came down in the east of the country, says Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. A Kh-101 cruise missile near Nowy Lipowiec. Another missile near Rudnik nad Sanem. Nobody was hurt. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called it a likely intentional provocation. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte called it a grave violation of Polish airspace. Warsaw asked for more troops and equipment for NATO's Eastern Sentry mission. It did not invoke Article Four of the NATO treaty, the clause for consultations when an ally feels threatened. Russia did not comment. For you, every incident like this tests what NATO's promise of mutual defence really covers. Next: the Gulf, and a weekend of fire.

Number one: Iran and the Gulf. The week began with a third American carrier. Axios, citing a U.S. official, reported the USS Theodore Roosevelt had arrived in the region. It joins the George H. W. Bush and the George Washington. Gulf News called it the biggest U.S. naval presence there since April. Then, on Monday, CNN reported that U.S. intelligence indicates Iran is developing plans to potentially use a dirty bomb or a chemical weapon against senior officials in Washington. Officials disagree on whether Iran can or will try. Iran's foreign ministry called the reports baseless. On Friday, Trump threatened military action if Tehran pursued such a plan. On Saturday night, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said missiles and drones targeted two U.S. Patriot radars at bases in Bahrain. Bahrain said it intercepted several attacks. A civilian industrial site caught fire, and nobody was hurt. The radar claims could not be verified. At sea, Britain's maritime agency UKMTO reported two tankers hit by unknown projectiles near Khasab in Oman, the second day in a row. Iran's army said a ship had hit a mine. And then Kharg Island, Iran's main oil terminal. Euronews and Iran International, citing satellite images and ship tracking, report more than fourteen tankers lined up for a convoy, to test the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports. Iran's deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, calls the blockade an act of war. Why it matters to you: about a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

What happens next. In the Gulf, everything turns on that convoy. Iran warned of a fierce military response if the U.S. military stops it, Iran International reports. No Iranian official has confirmed that it has sailed, although a deputy parliament speaker, Hamidreza Haji-Babaei, said on Saturday that tankers were already moving. Earlier this month, Trump told CNBC that restarting the war was highly unlikely, but he did not rule out more strikes. In Europe, NATO has not yet said whether it will send Poland more forces. Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera say Article Five would come into play after a sustained attack, not a single incident. In Yemen, the government is digging trenches and setting up checkpoints around Aden, Reuters reports. And the nuclear dialogue promised in Shenzhen still has no date. So, will Iran's tanker convoy try to break the U.S. blockade before the end of November? Tell us in the comments: yes or no.
Next Wednesday: NATO's Article Five. What does an attack on one really oblige the allies to do? In seventy-seven years, it has been invoked only once.

upload.title: Missiles in Poland, Fire in Bahrain: The Week's Top 5
upload.description:
The five biggest geopolitical stories of November 16 to 22, 2026, ranked by impact: Israeli tanks crossing Gaza's Yellow Line ceasefire boundary near Nuseirat and Bureij; Yemen's Houthis advancing toward Aden after government forces left the Bab al-Mandab coast; the Trump–Xi–Putin Shenzhen summit and its Declaration toward Peace on nuclear risk; Ukraine's strikes on the Kerch Bridge, Russia's mass attack on Kyiv and Russian missiles landing in Poland; and the Iran–U.S. standoff in the Gulf, from a third U.S. aircraft carrier and the reported dirty bomb plot to IRGC-claimed attacks on U.S. bases in Bahrain, tankers hit near Khasab and a reported tanker convoy at Kharg Island said to be preparing to test the U.S. blockade. Every claim is attributed to the source that reported it; unverified claims are labelled as such. Map locations are approximate.
